gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the ALLPOWERS P1800's XT60 solar input stops at 13 A (11–60 V, 650 W). The included panel's operating current at its working voltage therefore sets the recharge rate, not the watts on its label. ALLPOWERS also sells the same P1800 with a 600 W panel for $798, which ChatGPT never surfaced, and that kit pairs more solar with the same 1,024 Wh battery than the 400 W kit it picked.
standout_why: Pages compared: Trek4Tech (cited), runtimemath.com, solarpanelx.com and the cited theoutageplan.com, which would not load (SSL certificate error). Trek4Tech says 'the station's max solar input clips anything above it' and tells readers to check voltage and current limits, but it gives no volts or amps for any station and doesn't cover the P1800. Runtimemath applies a 13 A limit only to the ALLPOWERS R1500 + SP039 ('holds this 44 V panel to about 572 W'), not the P1800. SolarPanelX gives voltage windows but no current limits and doesn't say the input clips the bundled panel. No page links the P1800's 13 A input to its 400 W and 600 W kits, so rivals have the general idea but not this pairing. That makes it 2, not 3.
decides: This changes the pick inside the same brand. ChatGPT chose the P1800 + 400 W kit ($698) at about 3.4–4.3 h. The same station is sold with a 600 W panel for $798, and its 650 W input has room for that panel up to the 13 A limit. So the 600 W kit refills the same 1,024 Wh battery faster from its own panel, and the 13 A limit is the one figure that says how much faster. The exact cut depends on the 600 W panel's working voltage (see unsourced). As a guide, a panel working at 44 V would be held to 13 A × 44 V = 572 W. At that rate the battery needs about 1.8 h of strong sun before losses (1,024 Wh ÷ 572 W), against about 2.6 h at a full 400 W.
